hook_text: In 1945, there were a handful of atomic bombs. Forty years later, there were about seventy thousand. How did that happen?
clip_script: 1949. The Soviet Union tests an atomic bomb. America is shocked and builds something bigger: the hydrogen bomb, about 700 times the power of Hiroshima. The Soviets build one too. Then a Soviet bomb more than 3 000 times as powerful. Then rockets that cross the world in thirty minutes. Then submarines that hide under the sea. Each side builds because it fears the other. In American classrooms, children dive under desks in drills. Then, October 1962. A spy plane spots Soviet missiles in Cuba, right next to the United States. For thirteen days, the world holds its breath. Then the Soviets agree to take them away. The scare changes everything. Leaders install a hotline, ban tests in the air, and in 1987 destroy a whole class of missiles. The race made everyone less safe. Talking made them safer.
visual_style: A counter ticking up from 2 to 70 000; mushroom clouds of growing size; a rocket launch; children crouched under school desks; a reconnaissance photograph of missile sites in Cuba; two leaders shaking hands over a signed treaty.
pacing: Accelerating escalation, a held breath for the crisis, then a calmer close.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson to understand the arms race and how the world stepped back from the brink.
